title: Request & response anatomy
objectives: Read a raw HTTP request and response: request line, status line, header fields, the empty line and the body
Classify a method as safe and/or idempotent (RFC 9110), and say which failed requests a client may resend on its own
Tell `Content-Type` from `Accept`, and handle a response by its status class — `fetch` resolves on a 404 or a 500
Make a `POST` retry-safe with one `Idempotency-Key` per operation, retrying only failures that can succeed later

sources.title: Fetch Standard: extracting a body (default Content-Type)
IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field

questions.prompt: In a raw HTTP/1.1 request, how does the receiver know where the header fields end and the body begins?

options.text: An empty line — CR LF on its own — ends the header section
The `Content-Length` line is always the last header
A `Body:` header introduces the body
The first line that starts with `{` or `<` is the body

questions.explanation: The message is start line, header lines, **an empty line**, then the body (RFC 9112, section 2.1). Header order isn't fixed, so `Content-Length` can appear anywhere among them — its job is to say *how many bytes* of body follow the empty line, not where the headers stop. Nothing about the body's first character is consulted.

questions.prompt: Your client sends a JSON body to `POST /reports` and wants the report back as CSV. Which headers say that?

options.text: `Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: text/csv`
`Content-Type: text/csv` and `Accept: application/json`
`Content-Type: application/json, text/csv`
Only `Accept: text/csv` — the server can tell the body is JSON by looking at it

questions.explanation: `Content-Type` describes the body of the message it's on — here, the JSON you're sending. `Accept` is a request header listing what you'd like *back*. Swapping them is the classic mix-up. And servers don't sniff: body parsers such as Express's `express.json()` decide from `Content-Type` alone, so a JSON body labelled anything else is treated as not-JSON.

questions.prompt: Your `POST` gets back status `471`, a code you've never seen. Per RFC 9110, how should a client treat it?

options.text: Like `400 Bad Request` — the first digit says the request is the problem, so don't resend it unchanged
As success, since it isn't a `5xx`
As transient: retry with backoff until you get a code you recognise
As a network error, because unregistered codes are invalid

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 requires a client to understand the *class* of any status and treat an unrecognised code as the `x00` of its class — its own example is exactly `471` → `400`. The class tells you whose problem it is: `4xx` means the request as sent, so a retry of the same bytes gets the same answer. Only codes outside 100–599 are invalid, and those are treated as `5xx`.

questions.prompt: `DELETE /orders/7` returns `204`. A retry of the same request returns `404`. Is `DELETE` still idempotent?

options.text: Yes — idempotency is about the effect on the server (order 7 is gone either way), not about getting the same response
No — the two responses differ, so the method isn't idempotent here
Only if the server is fixed to return `204` both times
The question doesn't apply: `DELETE` is a safe method

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines idempotent as "the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests ... is the same as the effect for a single such request", and adds that the response might differ. Returning `404` the second time is fine. `DELETE` is idempotent but **not** safe — it asks for a state change; it just asks for the same one every time.

questions.prompt: The connection drops before any response arrives. Which request may an HTTP client library resend **automatically**, with no other information?

options.text: `PUT /profile` with the full profile in the body
`POST /orders` with the cart in the body
`PATCH /cart` with `{ "op": "add", "sku": "TEA-1" }`
Any of them — a dropped connection means the server never received it

questions.explanation: `PUT` is idempotent: if the first one landed, repeating it leaves the profile the same. `POST` and `PATCH` aren't (an `add` applied twice adds two), and RFC 9110 says a client SHOULD NOT retry those automatically without some way to know it's safe. The last option is the dangerous assumption: a dropped connection can happen *after* the server did the work and before the response got back.

questions.prompt: `GET /emails/42?action=archive` archives the email. A chat app's link-preview bot fetches pasted URLs, and users' emails start disappearing. Whose bug is it?

options.text: The server's: `GET` is safe, so an unsafe action must not be reachable through it — make it `POST /emails/42/archive`
The bot's: well-behaved bots don't follow URLs with query strings
The bot's: it should send `Cache-Control: no-store`
Nobody's, as long as the link includes a CSRF token

questions.explanation: Safe methods exist so that crawlers, prefetchers and preview bots can follow links without harm. RFC 9110 puts the burden on the resource owner: if parameters in the URL select an unsafe action, the owner MUST disable that action for safe methods. No header or token changes that — the bot was allowed to send that `GET`.

questions.prompt: A retry loop runs `const key = crypto.randomUUID()` *inside* the loop, then sends `POST /payments` with `Idempotency-Key: key`. The first attempt charges the card but its response is lost; the second succeeds. How many charges?

options.text: Two — each attempt carries a new key, so the server sees two different operations
One — the server dedupes any request that has an `Idempotency-Key` header
One — HTTP dedupes retried `POST`s on the same connection
Zero — the server rejects a payment whose key changed

questions.explanation: The key only works if it's the **same** on every attempt of one operation: the server stores "key `k1` → this response" and recognises the retry by `k1`. Minting a key per attempt gives each retry a fresh identity, so the header is present and protects nothing. Generate the key once, before the loop (or once per user action). HTTP itself never dedupes anything.

questions.prompt: Your server completed `Idempotency-Key: k1` for `{"amount": 40}`. Now `k1` arrives again with `{"amount": 50}`. What should it do?

options.text: Reject it (the IETF draft says `422`): one key must never be reused for a different request
Replay the stored `201` for the 40 charge
Process the 50 charge as a new payment
`409 Conflict`, the same answer as a retry that arrives while the first is still running

questions.explanation: A key identifies one operation, so a different payload under the same key is a client bug. Replaying the 40 response would tell the client its 50 charge succeeded; processing it would make keys meaningless. The Idempotency-Key Internet-Draft reserves `409` for "the original request is still being processed" and `422` for key reuse with a different payload — and it's why servers store a fingerprint of the request alongside the key.

prompts.prompt: Write the request line's method, and the header that asks for JSON back.
prompts.explanation: The request line is `method target version`. `Accept` is the request header for "what I want back"; `Content-Type` would describe a body, and this `GET` has none.

prompts.prompt: The server created order 43. Fill in the status code and the header that gives the new resource's URL.
prompts.explanation: RFC 9110 (section 9.3.3): when a `POST` creates a resource, the server SHOULD send `201 Created` with a `Location` header identifying it. The empty line before the JSON is what ends the headers.

prompts.prompt: Without this header, `fetch` labels the string body `text/plain;charset=UTF-8` and a JSON body parser skips it.
prompts.explanation: The Fetch standard gives a string body the type `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`; it never inspects the string. Express 5's `express.json()` only parses a matching `Content-Type`, so without this line `req.body` is `undefined`.

prompts.prompt: `fetch` resolved with a 500. Turn that into an error.
prompts.explanation: `res.ok` is `true` only for 200–299. `fetch` rejects when it has no response to give (network failure, CORS block, abort) — a `404` or `500` resolves normally and must be checked.

prompts.prompt: Make the retry safe, and wait as long as the server asked.
code: const key = crypto.randomUUID(); // once per operation
prompts.explanation: The same `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt lets the server recognise the retry. `Retry-After` (RFC 9110, section 10.2.3) on a `503` or `429` says how long to wait; its value is either seconds (as assumed here) or an HTTP date.

snippets.question: What does the client log?
snippets.explanation: No `Content-Type` was set, so `fetch` sent the string as `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`. `express.json()` skips anything that isn't `application/json`, leaving `req.body` as `undefined` (Express 5), and `JSON.stringify({ got: undefined })` drops the key — the response is `{}`. No error anywhere: the request "worked". Add `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }` and the server echoes `{"got":{"sku":"TEA-1"}}` (checked against Express 5.3.0).

snippets.question: What string does the client receive?
acceptable: the JSON without its closing brace
one byte short — the final } is missing
snippets.explanation: `body.length` counts UTF-16 code units: 15. `Content-Length` counts bytes, and `é` is two bytes in UTF-8, so the body is 16 bytes. The client reads exactly the 15 it was promised and stops — the closing `}` never arrives, and `JSON.parse` fails on the client, far from the bug. Use `Buffer.byteLength(body)` (or let the framework set the length). Verified with Node 24 and both `fetch` and curl.
